newsitem.title: VATICAN: Vatican blasts Australia euthanasia as horrific.
newsitem.headline: Vatican blasts Australia euthanasia as horrific.

text.p: The Vatican voiced horror on Thursday at the world's first legally-assisted suicide, saying no law or human suffering could justify euthanasia.
"One remains stupified and horrified by this shocking case of euthanasia that was requested and granted," said Father Gino Concetti, a Vatican moral theologian close to Pope John Paul.
He was reacting to the case of an elderly cancer patient who became the first person to take his life under a unique voluntary euthanasia law in Australia's Northern Territory.
The man, Bob Dent, died by a computer-delivered lethal injection in Darwin on Sunday after persuading doctors that his case was hopeless and he knew what he was doing.
"No law of the state can justify euthanasia. This would mean the end of human civilisation based on love and justice," Concetti told Reuters.

Concetti said those opposed to euthanasia had to react strongly to the Australian death. Concetti had expected to publish an editorial condemning the case in the Vatican newspaper L'Osservatore Romano on Thursday but it will appear in the paper at a later date.
"We must rail against the culture of death because life, even that which is in a terminal state because of an atrocious and incurable illness, is inviolable and sacred," Concetti said.
The Roman Catholic Church teaches that life begins at the moment of conception and ends at the moment of natural death.
The Church bans active euthanasia but does allow families to refuse or interrupt the use of life-supporting equipment in cases where patients are terminally ill.
In his 1995 encyclical Evangelium Vitae (The Gospel of Life), the Pope branded abortion and euthanasia as evils no man could justify and urged all Christians to oppose them.
Saying life had to be respected "at all costs", Concetti asserted that the Church's position against euthanasia was not insensitive to the suffering of the terminally ill.
"Nonetheless, it is unacceptable that a person decides to take his own life or procure one's own death," Concetti said.

Darwin doctor Philip Nitschke told Reuters he had helped Dent administer a lethal injection on Sunday. It was the first time that the Northern Territory's euthanasia law had been successfully used since it came into operation on July 1.
Dent, in an emotional open letter written on the eve of his death, said that he had been living on a "roller-coaster of pain" and would have killed himself with a gun if he had one.
Concetti rejected assertions by proponents of euthanasia that a life reduced to pain was essentially worthless.
"Pain can be relieved by the appropriate drugs and...in Christian teaching it can even be the means for the redemption of the individual and for others," Concetti said.
Dent, in his last letter on the topic that has bitterly divided Australians and people around the world, said the Church should not be allowed to influence laws on euthanasia.

"The Church and state should be kept separate," Dent wrote. "What right has anyone because of their own religious faith, to which I don't subscribe, to demand that I behave according to their rules and endure unnecessary intractable pain."
